title: HPSC Food Safety Officer — Unit 2: Food Microbiology, Spoilage and Preservation — 100-Question Practice Bank
coverage: Module 1: Food-borne bacteria — taxonomy, physiology, pathogenesis and foodborne disease classification
Module 4: Microbial destruction and thermal-death kinetics
Module 7: Moisture reduction and hurdle technology
Module 8: Chemical preservatives and food irradiation dosimetry
exam_alignment_note: This bank is an MCQ-based topic practice set, not an exact reproduction or prediction of an HPSC paper. The October 2023 HPSC FSO paper available for review used four alternatives and direct factual/conceptual single-best-answer questions in its Food Safety Standards & Nutrition section. However, reports of the HPSC FSO Advt. 25/2026 scheme dated 16.10.2026 describe a separate Screening Test (if held) and a 150-mark, 3-hour subjective Subject Knowledge Test; the Screening Test is reported as general studies/Haryana GK rather than a unit-wise food-microbiology paper. Therefore these 100 MCQs are best used for technical recall and concept testing, not as a claim about the format of the 2026 Subject Knowledge Test. Confirm the latest scheme and syllabus directly on hpsc.gov.in.
source_and_currency_note: Question content is primarily grounded in the uploaded Unit 2 master study manual. The manual explicitly distinguishes reported historical course wording from scientifically corrected interpretation and warns that approximate physiological values, historical textbook values and international benchmarks must not be presented as current Indian statutory requirements without checking the applicable FSSAI regulation, food category, amendment and notification. No current legal maximum has been invented in this bank.

Common examination traps explicitly identified in the source manual

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Food-borne intoxication
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: The consumer ingests toxin already formed in the food, so the illness is an intoxication. In infection, viable organisms are ingested and establish infection; in toxicoinfection, viable organisms are ingested and produce the clinically important toxin in the intestine. The short onset is compatible with preformed staphylococcal enterotoxin but incubation alone is not diagnostic.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Foodborne disease classification.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Clostridium perfringens food poisoning
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: In classical C. perfringens food poisoning, viable cells are ingested and sporulate in the intestine, where CPE is produced and released. Staphylococcal poisoning, food-borne botulism and emetic B. cereus illness are classically intoxications caused by preformed toxins in food.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Foodborne disease classification.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Cell-envelope properties affecting retention of the crystal-violet–iodine complex
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Gram staining reflects cell-envelope architecture and differential retention of the crystal-violet–iodine complex during decolourisation. It does not directly test pathogenicity, sporulation, motility or oxygen requirement. Gram-positive bacteria generally retain the primary stain; Gram-negative cells are decolourised and take the counterstain.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Bacterial physiology.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Oxygen released during decomposition of hydrogen peroxide
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Catalase catalyses 2H₂O₂ → 2H₂O + O₂. The visible bubbles are oxygen. Catalase protects cells against hydrogen peroxide, a reactive oxygen species. A positive catalase reaction is not proof of pathogenicity or aerobic growth.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Bacterial physiology.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: It detects activity associated with particular cytochrome-c-dependent respiratory systems
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: The oxidase reagent detects activity associated with certain cytochrome-c oxidase systems. It does not test all respiration. Acinetobacter is an important food-microbiology example of an aerobic organism that is typically oxidase-negative.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Bacterial physiology.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Acinetobacter — oxidase-negative; many Pseudomonas — oxidase-positive
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Acinetobacter is typically Gram-negative, catalase-positive and oxidase-negative, and is conventionally non-motile. Many familiar food-associated Pseudomonas are Gram-negative, oxidase-positive and motile. Neither genus forms bacterial endospores.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Bacterial physiology.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Facultative anaerobe
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Facultative anaerobes can grow with or without oxygen, switching metabolic pathways according to conditions. E. coli, Salmonella, Listeria and S. aureus are common examples. A microaerophile prefers oxygen below atmospheric concentration; an obligate anaerobe requires sufficiently anaerobic conditions.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Oxygen relationships.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Vacuum packaging changes microbial selection but is not a sterilising treatment
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Vacuum packaging lowers oxygen availability and suppresses many aerobic organisms, but it does not sterilise food. Facultative and anaerobic organisms, including LAB and Carnobacterium, may persist or grow. Anaerobic hazards require additional controls such as temperature, pH, water activity and validated processing.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Oxygen relationships.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: It is a dormant survival structure formed by certain bacteria
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: An endospore is a survival structure, not a reproductive structure. A vegetative cell ordinarily forms one endospore; germination and outgrowth produce a vegetative cell. Bacillus and Clostridium are important endospore-forming genera. Many Gram-positive organisms, including Listeria and Staphylococcus, are non-spore-formers.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Endospores.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Dehydrated core and calcium–dipicolinate
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Endospore resistance is multifactorial. A dehydrated core, calcium–dipicolinate, small acid-soluble spore proteins, cortex and coat structures, low metabolic activity and repair during return to growth all contribute. No single feature alone explains the full resistance.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Endospore resistance.

detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Two hours is 120 minutes, giving 120/30 = 4 generations. The multiplier is 2⁴ = 16; therefore 10³ × 16 = 1.6 × 10⁴ cells. This is an idealised calculation, not a prediction for all food-storage conditions.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Growth kinetics.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Extracellular proteases produced by psychrotrophic Pseudomonas before heat treatment remain active
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Psychrotrophic Pseudomonas can grow in raw chilled milk and produce extracellular proteases and lipases. A later heat treatment may kill cells without fully inactivating all previously produced enzymes. Residual proteolytic activity can contribute to bitterness and instability.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Pseudomonas and chilled spoilage.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Cereulide
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Cereulide is a cyclic dodecadepsipeptide produced by emetic B. cereus strains in food. It is relatively resistant to heat, acid and digestive proteolysis and acts as a potassium ionophore. Hbl, Nhe and CytK are associated with the diarrhoeal syndrome.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Bacillus cereus.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Diarrhoeal illness is classically a toxicoinfection; emetic illness is an intoxication
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: The classical diarrhoeal model involves viable cells/spores followed by enterotoxin production in the intestine (Hbl, Nhe, CytK), making it a toxicoinfection. Emetic illness follows ingestion of preformed cereulide in food and is an intoxication. The syndromes differ in toxin, site of production and usual incubation.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Bacillus cereus.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Cereulide is relatively heat-stable and may persist after vegetative cells are killed
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Emetic B. cereus strains can produce cereulide in food during improper holding. Cereulide is comparatively heat-stable, so reheating that kills vegetative cells may not inactivate toxin already formed. Prompt cooling and controlled storage prevent toxin accumulation.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Bacillus cereus.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Rope spoilage associated with Bacillus species
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Rope spoilage is commonly associated with Bacillus subtilis and related bacilli. Spores may survive baking, germinate in moist crumb and produce enzymes and extracellular polymers that break down crumb structure. It is bacterial spoilage, not necessarily mould growth.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Bread spoilage.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Refrigerated vacuum- or modified-atmosphere-packed meat and seafood
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Carnobacterium includes psychrotrophic lactic acid bacteria that can grow in chilled, vacuum- or modified-atmosphere-packed foods. Reduced oxygen suppresses many aerobic competitors but does not eliminate fermentative organisms. Some strains can contribute to spoilage or produce anti-Listeria bacteriocins.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Carnobacterium.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Anti-listerial activity alone is insufficient; strain-level safety and biogenic-amine production must be assessed
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Protective-culture suitability is strain- and food-specific. The strain must be evaluated for efficacy in the actual matrix, sensory effects, stability, resistance development and undesirable metabolites. Some strains decarboxylate tyrosine to tyramine, so beneficial antimicrobial activity does not establish universal safety.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Carnobacterium.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Slow cooling that permits surviving spores to germinate and vegetative cells to multiply
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: C. perfringens spores may survive cooking. Large food masses cool slowly, allowing germination and rapid vegetative growth. After ingestion, intestinal sporulation is associated with CPE production and diarrhoeal illness. Validated cooling, portioning and hot/cold holding are key controls.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Clostridium perfringens.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: During intestinal sporulation after ingestion
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: In classical C. perfringens food poisoning, CPE expression is strongly associated with sporulation in the intestine. Toxin released during mother-cell lysis binds susceptible claudin receptors, forms pores and injures intestinal epithelium. It is distinct from alpha toxin and beta toxin.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Clostridium perfringens.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Low-acid food, anaerobiosis and a permissive time–temperature history
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Low-acid hermetically sealed foods can provide anaerobic conditions. If spores survive and pH, water activity and temperature permit, growth and neurotoxin production may occur. The pH 4.6 boundary is a key low-acid canned-food classification/control concept, not a universal spore-killing or toxin-destruction condition.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Clostridium botulinum.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Food-borne botulism follows ingestion of preformed toxin, whereas infant botulism follows spore ingestion and intestinal toxin production
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Classical food-borne botulism is an intoxication: neurotoxin is formed in food before ingestion. Infant botulism is intestinal toxemia: ingested spores colonise the infant intestine and produce toxin there. Honey is a recognised preventable spore source and should not be given to infants under 12 months.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Clostridium botulinum.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: It can grow at refrigeration temperatures and persist in food-processing environments
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: L. monocytogenes is psychrotrophic, facultatively anaerobic and non-spore-forming. It can grow slowly at refrigeration temperatures, persist in processing niches and contaminate ready-to-eat foods after a lethality step. Freezing generally prevents multiplication but does not reliably eliminate it.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Listeria monocytogenes.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: ActA
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: ActA recruits host actin-polymerisation machinery, enabling intracellular movement and spread into adjacent cells. Listeriolysin O and phospholipases facilitate escape from the vacuole; they are not the principal actin-motility factor.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Listeria pathogenesis.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Low water activity can prevent growth while allowing viable Salmonella to survive
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Low water activity suppresses multiplication but does not guarantee microbial death. Salmonella can persist in low-moisture foods and may show increased heat resistance in such matrices. Validated lethality in the actual food and prevention of post-process contamination are essential.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Salmonella.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Preformed staphylococcal enterotoxin may persist after cells are killed
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: S. aureus can contaminate handled ready-to-eat foods and produce enterotoxin during growth. The toxin is relatively heat-stable compared with vegetative cells. Thus a later treatment may kill cells without reliably removing the hazard of preformed toxin.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Staphylococcus aureus.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: STEC/EHEC
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: STEC/EHEC produces Shiga toxins and can cause haemorrhagic colitis and haemolytic uraemic syndrome. The toxin A subunit inhibits protein synthesis by damaging the 28S rRNA of the 60S ribosomal subunit. ETEC causes secretory watery diarrhoea through LT/ST enterotoxins.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: E. coli pathotypes.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: 2 ATP
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: In classical homolactic fermentation, glucose is converted through glycolysis to two pyruvate molecules, which are reduced to lactate to regenerate NAD⁺. The net glycolytic yield is 2 ATP per glucose. The exact pathway and products depend on the LAB group and substrate.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Lactic acid bacteria.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Lactate, ethanol and carbon dioxide
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Obligately heterofermentative LAB use the phosphoketolase pathway. The classical product pattern includes lactate, ethanol and CO₂, with acetate replacing ethanol under some electron-acceptor conditions. The simplified net ATP yield is generally one ATP per glucose in the ethanol-forming route.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 1 — Food-borne bacteria, topic: Lactic acid bacteria.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: A conidium is a fungal asexual spore; a bacterial endospore is a bacterial survival structure
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Conidia are asexual fungal spores formed externally on specialised structures such as conidiophores. Bacterial endospores are dormant survival structures formed internally by certain bacteria. The terms are not interchangeable and have different biological functions.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 2 — Food-borne moulds and mycotoxins, topic: Mould morphology.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Most food-associated moulds are obligately aerobic
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Most food-associated filamentous moulds are aerobic and commonly grow at oxygenated surfaces. Oxygen availability can affect both fungal biomass and secondary metabolite production, including mycotoxin formation. Vacuum or modified atmosphere may be a hurdle but does not guarantee removal of mycotoxin risk.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 2 — Food-borne moulds and mycotoxins, topic: Mould ecology.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Osmophilic yeasts and xerophilic moulds
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: High sugar and acidity inhibit many bacteria but may select for osmotolerant/osmophilic yeasts and xerophilic moulds. Preservation hurdles change the microbial ecology rather than uniformly sterilising the food.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 2 — Food-borne moulds and mycotoxins, topic: Mould ecology.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Toxin production can have a different optimum from biomass formation
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Mycotoxin biosynthesis is secondary metabolism and depends on strain, substrate and environmental conditions. The optimum for toxin production may differ from the optimum for fungal biomass. Toxins can persist after the producing mould is no longer viable, and visible mould removal does not guarantee toxin removal.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 2 — Food-borne moulds and mycotoxins, topic: Mycotoxin biology.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Aspergillus parasiticus
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: A. parasiticus commonly produces both B- and G-series aflatoxins. A. flavus commonly produces B-series aflatoxins, although not every strain is toxigenic. Toxin production is strain-dependent; species identification alone is not proof of toxin concentration.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 2 — Food-borne moulds and mycotoxins, topic: Aflatoxins.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Terminal 8,9 double bond
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Aflatoxin B1 can be metabolically activated to the reactive 8,9-epoxide, which forms adducts with DNA and proteins. This is central to its genotoxic and carcinogenic action. The question tests the structural feature highlighted in the manual.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 2 — Food-borne moulds and mycotoxins, topic: Aflatoxins.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Carry-over of aflatoxin B1 from contaminated animal feed into milk
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Animals consuming feed contaminated with aflatoxin B1 can metabolise part of it to aflatoxin M1, which may be excreted in milk. Feed-quality control is therefore an important intervention for milk safety. Ordinary pasteurisation does not reliably eliminate AFM1.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 2 — Food-borne moulds and mycotoxins, topic: Aflatoxins.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Nephrotoxic potential
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Ochratoxin A is a mycotoxin produced by selected Aspergillus and Penicillium species. Its toxicological significance includes nephrotoxicity and other systemic effects. Producer identity and occurrence vary by species, strain and commodity.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 2 — Food-borne moulds and mycotoxins, topic: Ochratoxin A.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Apple juice and products from mould-damaged apples
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Patulin is associated particularly with Penicillium expansum and damaged or mouldy apples and apple juice. Sorting and removal of damaged fruit reduce risk, but ordinary juice pasteurisation does not guarantee patulin removal.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 2 — Food-borne moulds and mycotoxins, topic: Patulin.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Mycotoxins may have diffused beyond visible mould and may persist after fungal death
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Mycotoxins can remain in the commodity after fungal viability is lost and may not be confined to visibly mouldy portions. Control requires prevention, sorting, representative sampling, validated testing and appropriate handling. Physical removal alone is not proof of detoxification.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 2 — Food-borne moulds and mycotoxins, topic: Mycotoxin control.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Legal maximum levels are jurisdiction- and commodity-specific; current FSSAI schedules must be checked
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: The manual explicitly cautions that physiological values, historical textbook values and international benchmarks must not be presented as current Indian statutory requirements. The applicable FSSAI contaminant/toxin schedule, food category and amendments must be checked.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 2 — Food-borne moulds and mycotoxins, topic: Mycotoxin regulation.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Harvest appropriately, dry promptly, prevent moisture ingress and monitor storage conditions
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Pre-harvest stress and insect damage can increase susceptibility, while poor post-harvest drying and storage permit mould growth and toxin production. Prompt drying, moisture control, clean storage, pest management, sorting and representative monitoring are complementary controls.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 2 — Food-borne moulds and mycotoxins, topic: Mould prevention.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Glucans, mannoproteins and chitin
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Yeasts are eukaryotic fungi. Their cell walls commonly contain glucans, mannoproteins and chitin; their membranes contain sterols, principally ergosterol. Peptidoglycan and lipopolysaccharide are bacterial envelope components.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 3 — Food-borne yeasts, topic: Yeast structure.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Budding
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Many food yeasts multiply by multilateral or polar budding: a bud forms, the nucleus divides and the daughter cell separates. Some yeasts also form sexual ascospores; these are fungal spores and are not bacterial endospores.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 3 — Food-borne yeasts, topic: Yeast reproduction.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Many yeasts can ferment in the absence of oxygen
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Many yeasts can ferment sugars anaerobically, although oxygen may increase biomass formation and change metabolic products. Their flexible physiology helps some species grow in acidic, sugary or low-oxygen foods where many bacteria are disadvantaged.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 3 — Food-borne yeasts, topic: Yeast physiology.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Osmophilic yeast fermentation
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: High sugar suppresses many bacteria but selects for osmophilic yeasts. Fermentation can produce carbon dioxide, gas, turbidity and off-flavours, sometimes before visible growth becomes obvious. High sugar is therefore not an absolute preservation barrier.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 3 — Food-borne yeasts, topic: Yeast spoilage.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Zygosaccharomyces bailii
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Zygosaccharomyces bailii is a notable spoilage yeast in acidic foods and can show resistance to weak-acid preservatives. Effective control requires appropriate formulation, hygiene, processing and packaging rather than assuming benzoate or sorbate will always prevent growth.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 3 — Food-borne yeasts, topic: Preservative resistance.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Salted meats, cheeses, brines and other high-salt environments
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: D. hansenii is salt-tolerant and can be found in salted meats, cheeses, brines and related environments. The manual specifically corrects the misconception that it occurs only in dairy products.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 3 — Food-borne yeasts, topic: Yeast ecology.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Visible colonies on the food surface
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Yeast spoilage may present as gas, off-flavour, turbidity or package swelling without obvious surface colonies. Visible growth is not a necessary condition for recognising spoilage.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 3 — Food-borne yeasts, topic: Yeast spoilage.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: They may select acid-tolerant and osmotolerant yeasts
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Low pH and high sugar are selective hurdles. Some yeasts tolerate acidity and osmotic stress, accumulate compatible solutes such as glycerol and ferment without oxygen. Product-specific hurdle combinations and process validation are required.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 3 — Food-borne yeasts, topic: Yeast preservation.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Reduce a microbial population by 90% or one log cycle
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: D is the time at a specified temperature and in a specified matrix required for a one-log (90%) reduction in survivors. It is not absolute sterilisation. D-values depend on organism, temperature, food composition, pH, water activity and other process conditions.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 4 — Microbial destruction and thermal-death kinetics, topic: D-value.

detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Six minutes represents 6/2 = 3 decimal reductions. The population falls from 10⁶ to 10³. This calculation assumes log-linear inactivation and constant process conditions; real survivor curves can show shoulders or tailing.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 4 — Microbial destruction and thermal-death kinetics, topic: D-value calculation.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Temperature and food matrix
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: D-values are not universal constants for a species. They must be associated with a specified temperature and matrix because fat, salt, sugar, protein, pH, water activity, spore state and heating method can change thermal resistance.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 4 — Microbial destruction and thermal-death kinetics, topic: D-value.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Reduce the D-value by one log cycle
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: The z-value is the temperature change that produces a tenfold change in D-value. It is obtained from the log D versus temperature relationship and is expressed in degrees Celsius, not minutes. A smaller z-value indicates greater temperature sensitivity.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 4 — Microbial destruction and thermal-death kinetics, topic: z-value.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: F-value is equivalent lethality time at a reference temperature; D-value is time for one-log reduction at a stated temperature
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: D describes the time for one decimal reduction at a specified temperature. F expresses equivalent time at a reference temperature for a defined lethality. For a constant-temperature process, F can be related to D multiplied by the number of decimal reductions.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 4 — Microbial destruction and thermal-death kinetics, topic: F-value.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: 1 min
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: The relative lethality is 10^[(111.1−121.1)/10] = 10⁻¹ = 0.1. F₀ = time × relative lethality = 10 × 0.1 = 1 minute. F₀ integrates lethality relative to the reference temperature; it is not simply the physical holding time.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 4 — Microbial destruction and thermal-death kinetics, topic: F0 calculation.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: 2.52 min
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Under the stated classical assumptions, 12 × 0.21 = 2.52 minutes of equivalent lethality at 121.1°C. This is a theoretical derivation, not a universal scheduled process for every low-acid canned food. Actual processes require product- and container-specific validation.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 4 — Microbial destruction and thermal-death kinetics, topic: 12D process.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Absence of microorganisms capable of growing under normal non-refrigerated storage and distribution conditions, with process and package integrity considered
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Commercial sterility is not absolute sterility. It is a process-and-product concept intended to prevent growth of organisms of public-health significance or spoilage concern under normal storage and distribution. Hermetic sealing and validated processing are essential.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 4 — Microbial destruction and thermal-death kinetics, topic: Commercial sterility.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: It is the slowest-heating location and may receive the least lethality
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Heat penetration is not uniform in all products and containers. The cold spot is the location that heats most slowly or receives the least accumulated lethality. Process validation must consider container geometry, product properties, fill, headspace and heating behaviour.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 4 — Microbial destruction and thermal-death kinetics, topic: Thermal processing.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: A resistant subpopulation or protective microenvironment survives longer
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Tailing can result from heterogeneous resistance, clumping, protective food particles or a resistant subpopulation. It means the ideal straight-line log-linear model may not describe the entire inactivation curve. Validation must account for actual survival behaviour.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 4 — Microbial destruction and thermal-death kinetics, topic: Survivor curves.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: High fat, sugar or salt under some conditions
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Food matrix effects can materially alter thermal resistance. High fat may protect cells by reducing water contact, while high sugar or salt can lower water activity and increase resistance. Protein and clumps may also protect. The effect is matrix-specific, so lethality data cannot be transferred blindly.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 4 — Microbial destruction and thermal-death kinetics, topic: Thermal resistance.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Slow metabolic and growth rates and often extend lag time
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Chilling generally slows enzyme activity, membrane transport and microbial growth, often extending lag time and shelf life. It is not a universal lethal treatment. Psychrotrophic organisms such as Listeria and some spoilage bacteria may still grow during prolonged refrigerated storage.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 5 — Low-temperature preservation, topic: Chilling.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Psychrotrophs can grow at refrigeration temperatures but commonly have a warmer optimum, often around 20–30°C
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Psychrotrophs are able to grow at refrigeration temperatures but their optimum is commonly warmer, often around 20–30°C. Psychrophiles are adapted to low temperatures and often have lower optima. Growth threshold and optimum temperature are different parameters.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 5 — Low-temperature preservation, topic: Psychrotrophs.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Freezing generally inhibits growth but many microorganisms survive
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Freezing converts water to ice and reduces available liquid water, greatly inhibiting microbial multiplication. It does not reliably destroy all microorganisms or toxins. Chemical and enzymatic changes can continue slowly, and survivors may grow after thawing.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 5 — Low-temperature preservation, topic: Freezing.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Usually produces smaller ice crystals and less structural damage
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Rapid freezing generally forms smaller crystals and causes less tissue disruption than slow freezing. However, intracellular ice can itself be damaging and crystal location depends on freezing rate, cell type and matrix. It is incorrect to say quick freezing always produces harmless intracellular ice.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 5 — Low-temperature preservation, topic: Freezing injury.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Surviving microorganisms may multiply as the food warms, especially at the surface
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Thawing can create temperature gradients, with the surface warming while the centre remains frozen. Surviving organisms may multiply in the thawed region. Thawing can also cause drip loss, nutrient loss and recrystallisation; controlled thawing is important.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 5 — Low-temperature preservation, topic: Thawing.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Many pathogens can survive frozen storage even when they do not multiply
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Freezing usually prevents or greatly slows multiplication, but pathogens can remain viable. After thawing, they may resume growth if conditions permit. Freezing should therefore be considered a growth-control hurdle, not a validated kill step.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 5 — Low-temperature preservation, topic: Frozen storage.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: It limits growth of organisms that may multiply slowly under refrigeration
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Cold-chain control reduces growth rate and delays population increase, but does not eliminate organisms such as L. monocytogenes. It must be combined with hygienic design, prevention of post-lethality contamination, shelf-life control and validated formulation.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 5 — Low-temperature preservation, topic: Cold chain.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: LAB and psychrotrophic facultative or anaerobic organisms
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Reduced oxygen suppresses many aerobic spoilage organisms and changes competitive ecology. LAB and Carnobacterium may grow in vacuum or modified-atmosphere foods. Non-proteolytic C. botulinum is also an important hazard in some chilled anaerobically packaged foods if other controls fail.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 5 — Low-temperature preservation, topic: Low-temperature selection.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Inactivate quality-degrading enzymes and reduce surface microbial load
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Blanching is a mild heat treatment used principally to inactivate enzymes such as peroxidase, catalase, polyphenol oxidase and lipoxygenase, reduce surface flora, remove intercellular gases and prepare tissues for subsequent processing. It is not a commercial sterilisation step.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 6 — High-temperature preservation, topic: Blanching.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Relatively heat-resistant and difficult to inactivate in some vegetables
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Peroxidase is relatively heat-resistant compared with several quality-degrading enzymes, so its residual activity can be used as an indicator of blanching adequacy in selected vegetables. A blanching test is an enzyme-control test, not proof of commercial sterility.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 6 — High-temperature preservation, topic: Blanching.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: LTLT 62.8°C/30 min; HTST 71.7°C/15 s
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: The manual gives the classical LTLT/batch schedule as 62.8°C for 30 minutes and HTST as 71.7°C for 15 seconds. These are classic reference schedules; current legal standards may recognise additional validated methods. They should not be used to imply that all spores or heat-stable toxins are destroyed.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 6 — High-temperature preservation, topic: Pasteurisation.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Consistent with adequate pasteurisation, assuming test validity
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Alkaline phosphatase is naturally present in raw milk and is more heat-resistant than many milk-borne vegetative pathogens. Adequate pasteurisation should inactivate it below the validated detection threshold. A negative test supports process adequacy but does not prove absence of post-process contamination.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 6 — High-temperature preservation, topic: Alkaline phosphatase.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Approximately 135–150°C for a few seconds
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: The manual corrects the reported historical figure of 93.4°C for 3 seconds. UHT commonly operates around 135–150°C for a few seconds, using a validated process followed by aseptic packaging. UHT treatment and aseptic packaging work together to achieve commercial sterility.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 6 — High-temperature preservation, topic: UHT processing.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: It prevents recontamination after the high-temperature treatment
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: UHT treatment reduces viable microorganisms, but the product can be recontaminated during filling if packaging and filling conditions are not aseptic. Commercial sterility therefore depends on the validated thermal process, sterile product path and package integrity.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 6 — High-temperature preservation, topic: UHT packaging.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Proteolytic Clostridium botulinum spores
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Low-acid hermetically sealed foods provide anaerobic conditions. Proteolytic C. botulinum spores are a central public-health target in retorting. A validated scheduled process must account for spore resistance, heat penetration, cold spots and container integrity.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 6 — High-temperature preservation, topic: Retorting.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: A cold spot in the product receives insufficient accumulated lethality
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Retort temperature does not equal product cold-spot temperature. Container size, geometry, viscosity, convection/conduction, fill weight and come-up time affect heat penetration. Validation must demonstrate adequate lethality at the slowest-heating location.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 6 — High-temperature preservation, topic: Retorting.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Validated retorting
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Retorting uses a validated high-temperature process to achieve commercial sterility in hermetically sealed foods, including control of relevant spores. Refrigeration and pasteurisation are not equivalent spore-destruction processes; blanching principally targets enzymes.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 6 — High-temperature preservation, topic: Thermal process comparison.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Pasteurisation may destroy vegetative pathogens but leave spores and some heat-stable toxins
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Thermal processes act differently on vegetative cells, spores, toxins and enzymes. Pasteurisation targets specified vegetative pathogens and spoilage organisms but does not destroy all spores or all heat-stable toxins. Package integrity and post-process hygiene remain important.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 6 — High-temperature preservation, topic: Thermal targets.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Blanching
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Blanching inactivates enzymes that could otherwise remain active during frozen storage and cause colour, flavour and texture deterioration. It is followed by cooling or subsequent processing and then freezing. Underblanching leaves residual enzyme activity; overblanching damages quality.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 6 — High-temperature preservation, topic: Thermal process selection.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Commercial sterility allows controlled survival of organisms unable to grow under normal intended storage conditions
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Commercial sterility is defined in relation to organisms capable of growing under normal non-refrigerated storage and distribution conditions and the integrity of the sealed package. It is not a claim that no viable organism exists under every possible laboratory condition.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 6 — High-temperature preservation, topic: Commercial sterility.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Ratio of water vapour pressure above food to that above pure water at the same temperature
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Water activity (a_w) is p/p₀, where p is the vapour pressure above the food and p₀ is the vapour pressure above pure water at the same temperature. It describes thermodynamic availability of water, not simply total moisture content.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 7 — Moisture reduction and hurdle technology, topic: Water activity.

detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: At equilibrium, ERH (%) is approximately 100 times water activity. Thus a food with a_w = 0.80 equilibrates with approximately 80% relative humidity. The relationship assumes equilibrium and the same temperature.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 7 — Moisture reduction and hurdle technology, topic: Water activity.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Their water activities may differ because solutes alter vapour pressure and water availability
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Moisture content is the amount of water; a_w reflects its thermodynamic availability. Solutes such as salt, sucrose, glucose syrup and glycerol reduce a_w. Equal moisture content does not imply equal a_w because food composition and water binding differ.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 7 — Moisture reduction and hurdle technology, topic: Water activity.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Multiplication of ordinary food-associated microorganisms is generally prevented, but viable cells or spores may remain
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: The manual gives approximately a_w 0.60 as a practical lower boundary for multiplication of ordinary food-associated microorganisms. Below this, growth is generally prevented, but cells, spores and toxins may survive, and chemical deterioration can continue.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 7 — Moisture reduction and hurdle technology, topic: Water activity.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Equilibrium moisture content against water activity at a fixed temperature
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: A moisture sorption isotherm describes the relationship between equilibrium moisture content and a_w at a fixed temperature. Adsorption and desorption curves may not coincide; this phenomenon is called hysteresis.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 7 — Moisture reduction and hurdle technology, topic: Sorption isotherms.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Hysteresis
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Hysteresis occurs because a food can contain different moisture levels at the same a_w depending on whether it is gaining or losing moisture. Capillary condensation, swelling, structural collapse and matrix changes can contribute.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 7 — Moisture reduction and hurdle technology, topic: Sorption isotherms.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: a_w approximately 0.60–0.85 and moisture often approximately 15–40%
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Intermediate moisture foods retain enough moisture for a soft or plastic texture while having reduced a_w, often around 0.60–0.85 depending on definition. Their stability depends on a combination of reduced a_w, pH, preservatives, packaging, heat and hygienic manufacture.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 7 — Moisture reduction and hurdle technology, topic: Intermediate moisture foods.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Combine several preservation factors that disrupt different microbial homeostatic systems
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Hurdle technology combines temperature, pH, a_w, redox potential, preservatives, competitive flora, modified atmosphere, packaging and heat, among others. Interactions can be synergistic, but the complete system must be validated because hurdles can interact and affect quality.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 7 — Moisture reduction and hurdle technology, topic: Hurdle technology.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Multiple stresses act on different microbial functions and may act synergistically
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Hurdles may act synergistically by disrupting proton balance, water balance, membranes, enzymes and repair systems. However, the order and interaction matter: low a_w can sometimes increase heat resistance, and packaging can create anaerobic conditions. Validation is essential.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 7 — Moisture reduction and hurdle technology, topic: Hurdle technology.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Localised high-a_w pockets caused by moisture migration
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Surface moisture migration can create local high-a_w niches even when average product a_w is low. These pockets may support mould growth or spoilage. Preservative redistribution, texture changes and chemical browning are additional limitations.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 7 — Moisture reduction and hurdle technology, topic: Hurdle technology.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: It is an important growth-control/classification boundary but does not prove spore destruction or toxin inactivation
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Equilibrium pH 4.6 is a key boundary in low-acid canned-food control because adequate acidification inhibits growth and toxin formation by the central proteolytic C. botulinum target. It does not kill all spores, destroy preformed toxin or eliminate acid-tolerant hazards.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 7 — Moisture reduction and hurdle technology, topic: Hurdle technology.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: The acid is predominantly undissociated at lower pH
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: The undissociated form of a weak acid can cross microbial membranes more readily. It dissociates in the higher-pH cytoplasm, causing intracellular acidification, anion accumulation and energy stress. Therefore efficacy depends strongly on pH, acid pKa, food matrix and organism.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 8 — Chemical preservatives and food irradiation, topic: Weak organic acids.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Henderson–Hasselbalch relationship
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: The Henderson–Hasselbalch relationship links pH, pKa and the ratio of dissociated to undissociated acid. It helps explain why a greater fraction of a weak organic acid is undissociated at lower pH, supporting membrane entry and antimicrobial activity.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 8 — Chemical preservatives and food irradiation, topic: Weak organic acids.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Nisin is a bacteriocin active mainly against susceptible Gram-positive bacteria; natamycin is antifungal
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Nisin is a bacteriocin produced by selected lactic acid bacteria and is mainly active against susceptible Gram-positive bacteria. Natamycin is an antifungal agent that targets fungal membrane sterols. Their spectra and applications differ, and neither is a universal preservative.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 8 — Chemical preservatives and food irradiation, topic: Biopreservatives.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Verify the current FSSAI regulation, food category, amendment and notification
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Preservative permissions and maximum levels are food-category-specific and may change through amendments. A historical value or international benchmark is not automatically a current Indian statutory requirement. The relevant FSSAI regulation and notification must be checked.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 8 — Chemical preservatives and food irradiation, topic: Preservative regulation.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Cobalt-60
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Cobalt-60 is a recognised gamma source for food irradiation. The manual also flags the common misprint 'Ce-137': the correct radionuclide is caesium-137 (Cs-137), while Ce denotes cerium.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 8 — Chemical preservatives and food irradiation, topic: Irradiation.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: It can damage microbial DNA directly and indirectly and does not make food radioactive when properly applied under approved conditions
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Ionising radiation damages microbial structures and DNA directly and through reactive species generated by water radiolysis. Approved irradiation does not make food radioactive. Effectiveness depends on absorbed dose, dose uniformity, target organism, food matrix and process validation.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 8 — Chemical preservatives and food irradiation, topic: Irradiation.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Radurisation — low-dose shelf-life extension; radicidation — reduction of specified pathogens
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Radurisation is a low-dose treatment concept used to extend shelf life by reducing spoilage organisms. Radicidation refers to reducing specified pathogens. Radappertisation is a high-dose commercial sterilisation concept, but should not be described as absolute sterility in every circumstance.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 8 — Chemical preservatives and food irradiation, topic: Irradiation terminology.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Gray (Gy)
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Absorbed dose is measured in gray: 1 Gy = 1 joule of energy absorbed per kilogram of matter. Food irradiation doses are commonly expressed in kilogray (kGy). Becquerel measures radioactive activity, while sievert is used for radiation protection dose quantities.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 8 — Chemical preservatives and food irradiation, topic: Irradiation dosimetry.

detailed_explanations.correct_answer: Sprout inhibition in bulbs and tubers
detailed_explanations.detailed_explanation: Sprout inhibition in commodities such as potatoes and onions generally uses lower doses than microbial decontamination applications such as spice treatment. Dose selection is commodity- and purpose-specific; dose mapping, uniformity, legal authorisation and verification are required.
detailed_explanations.source_basis: Uploaded Unit 2 master study manual — Module 8 — Chemical preservatives and food irradiation, topic: Irradiation applications.
